bib.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations

question: How should researchers compute uncertainty, compare models, reduce variance and plan sample size when analysing language model eval results as experiments?
hypothesis: Treating eval questions as draws from a super-population lets standard experiment-analysis statistics give rigorous error bars and significance tests for evals.
contributions: Standard errors via CLT, with clustered standard errors for grouped questions
Variance reduction by resampling and next-token probabilities; advice not to change temperature
Power analysis and sample-size formula with MDE

results.claim: Clustered standard errors on DROP are about 3x the naive CLT standard errors.
results.setup: Table 4: DROP, Anthropic models, ratio SE_clustered/SE_CLT (1.34 vs 0.44); model and run details not given
results.quote: Clustered and naive standard errors computed on two popular evals using Anthropic models (non-fictional numbers). Analyzing the same data, clustered standard errors can be over 3X larger than naive standard errors.

results.claim: Clustering inflates RACE-H standard error only slightly.
Under uniform difficulty and binary scores, resampling K times multiplies estimator variance by (1+2/K)/3; max reduction is 2/3.
results.setup: Binary scores, question difficulty x~U[0,1]; Var(x)=1/12, E[sigma^2]=1/6
results.quote: The upper limit on variance reduction via resampling in this example is 2/3.

results.claim: K=2 reduces variance by 1/3, K=4 by 1/2, K=6 by 5/9 in that example.
results.quote: Going from K = 1 (no resampling of answers) to K = 2, the total variance is reduced by 1/3. Increasing to K = 4, we have a variance reduction of 1/2, and setting K = 6, we reduce variance by 5/9.

results.claim: Analysing next-token probabilities removes conditional variance, matching the resampling limit of 2/3 variance reduction.
results.quote: Using the uniform-difficulty example from the previous section, next-token probabilities will reduce the variance of the estimator by 2/3 (the upper limit achievable via resampling) compared to grading a single sample from each question.

results.claim: Lowering temperature to 0 can triple the minimum variance (1/12 to 1/4).
results.setup: Single-token true/false eval, conditional means at T=1 ~U[0,1], T=0 rounds to Bernoulli(1/2)
results.quote: has inadvertently tripled the minimum variance in the score data from 1/12 to 1/4.

results.claim: With x~U[1/3,1], T=0 shifts the mean from 2/3 to 3/4 and raises variance of conditional means about five-fold.
results.quote: Then E[xT=1] = 2/3 < E[xT=0] = 3/4 and Var(xT=1) = 1/27 ≪Var(xT=0) = 3/16; that is, not only has the temperature change shifted the expected score, but the variance of the conditional means has increased approximately five-fold.

results.claim: Paired differences cut estimator variance by 1/3 when score correlation is 0.5 (uniform scores, zero conditional variance).
results.setup: Two models, continuous scores uniform on [0,1] from next-token probabilities, correlation 0.5
results.quote: will reduce the variance of the estimator by 1/3 in relative terms (that is, from 1/6 to 1/9 in absolute terms).

results.claim: Llama 3 report uses SE_Bernoulli for all evals, so its intervals are too wide for fractional scores and too narrow for clustered evals.
results.quote: We also note that [7] incorrectly estimates all of its standard errors using SEBernoulli, even when si takes fractional values, such as with an F1 score.

limits: Analytic treatment with fictional models and hypothetical numbers; only Table 4 uses real (Anthropic model) data, with no model, run or sample details stated.
Assumes questions are i.i.d. draws from a super-population, or clusters are independent; CLT needs finite variance and large n.
Next-token probability variance reduction does not apply to chain-of-thought evals.
Power inputs (omega^2, sigma^2) must be estimated from earlier data with K much greater than 1.
Does not judge the qualitative merits of evals; a reader is assumed to have some statistics training.
Examples assume uniform difficulty and independent question draws for simple closed forms.
Estimation of cluster-adjusted quantities with subsampling: sample whole clusters.
practices: Report the standard error of the mean in parentheses beneath each eval score, with the question count (Sec 2.1, Table 2).
Compute SE with the CLT formula, not SE_Bernoulli, when scores are fractional (Sec 2.1).
Bootstrapping is unnecessary unless the sampling scheme or estimator is complicated (Sec 2.1).
Use clustered standard errors when questions come in related groups, and report cluster count (Sec 2.2, Table 3).
Resample each question K times with K large enough that E[sigma^2]/K is much less than Var(x) and average per question; do not pool all K*N answers (Sec 3.1).
Use next-token probabilities when the eval can be run without generation (Sec 3.2).
Do not lower sampling temperature to cut variance (Sec 3.3).
Compare two models with paired question-level differences and report differences, SEs, CIs and correlations (Sec 4.2, Table 5).
Run power analysis to choose n, K, or find the MDE before running an eval (Sec 5).
